# Projects

## File Management {.fs70}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   [Projects]{.b .blue} are [special folders]{.b .green} on your computer
    -   They contain all files related to a task
    -   They keep everything together and organized

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Projects make it easy to [find and use your files]{.b .green}
    -   No need to specify long, annoying file paths
    -   No need to worry about working directories
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Projects make it easy to [switch between tasks]{.b .green}
    -   They will remember exactly where you left off
    -   You can even open multiple projects at once
:::
:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
{{< lif "../../icons/box.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::
:::

::: {.aside}
*Note.* Save your project in a cloud service folder (e.g., Box, Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive) to backup and sync it.
:::


## Creating a Project

-   [File > New Project...]{.b .blue}
    -   Choose [New Directory]{.b .blue}, then [New Project]{.b .blue}
    -   Name the directory after the course or the task
    -   Browse to where the folder should live

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   RStudio makes the folder and puts an [.Rproj file]{.b .green} inside it
    -   That file *is* the project; opening it opens the project
:::

## Working Inside a Project

-   The [Files]{.b .blue} tab (Extras pane) shows the project folder

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Make a new script and RStudio puts it [in the project folder]{.b .green}
    -   Add a line of text, such as `# Hello World`
    -   Save it; the dialog already points at the project folder
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Close the script with the [x]{.b .blue} icon, then reopen it from [Files]{.b .blue}
:::

## Closing and Reopening a Project

-   [File > Close Project]{.b .blue}
    -   The Source Editor empties and the Console resets
    -   It looks like your work is [gone]{.b .red}

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   [File > Open Project]{.b .blue}, then pick the [.Rproj]{.b .blue} file in your folder
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Everything comes [back exactly where you left it]{.b .green}
    -   Open files, working directory, and history are all restored
:::


# Quarto

## Quarto {.fs80}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   [Quarto](https://www.quarto.org) is a [technical publishing system]{.b .green}

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Create [dynamic content]{.b .blue} with R, Python, Julia, and Observable
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Articles, reports, slideshows, websites, blogs, and books in [HTML, PDF, MS Word, and ePub]{.b .blue} formats
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Include [equations, citations, crossrefs]{.b .blue}, panels, callouts, advanced layouts, etc.
:::
:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
{{< lif "../../icons/poetry.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::
:::


## Creating a Quarto Document

-   [File > New File > Quarto Document...]{.b .blue}
    -   Keep the defaults, then [Create Empty Document]{.b .blue}

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   [File > Save]{.b .blue}
    -   The dialog defaults to the project folder
    -   Give it a name and note the [.qmd]{.b .green} extension
:::

## Adding an R Chunk

-   A [chunk]{.b .blue} is a block of R code sitting inside the document
-   Any one of these will insert one:
    -   Click the [green box with a C and a plus sign]{.b .blue} (top-right)
    -   <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Alt</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd> (Win) or <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Option</kbd>+<kbd>I</kbd> (Mac)
    -   Type the [fences]{.b .blue} yourself: three backticks and `{r}`, then a
        closing line of three backticks

## Running Code in a Chunk

-   A chunk works like a [mini console]{.b .green}
    -   Do a calculation inside it, then click the [green arrow]{.b .blue}
    -   The answer appears [right below the chunk]{.b .green}

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Save and [render]{.b .blue} the document and the answer appears in the output too
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Chunk [options]{.b .blue} control how each chunk behaves; more later
:::


# Markdown

## Markdown

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   [Markdown](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html) is a simple [text-to-HTML]{.b .green} conversion language used by Quarto, GitHub, Obsidian, etc.

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   It will allow us to add [formatted text, images, links, lists]{.b .blue}, etc. to our Quarto documents
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Quarto will treat all text that is [not in a code chunk]{.b .green} as markdown
:::

:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
{{< lif "../../icons/text_box.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::
:::

## Formatting Text

| Type this | Get this |
|:---|:---|
| `*italics*` | *italics* |
| `**bold**` | **bold** |
| `***italics and bold***` | ***italics and bold*** |
| `superscript^2^` | superscript^2^ |
| `subscript~2~` | subscript~2~ |
| `~~strikethrough~~` | ~~strikethrough~~ |
| `` `verbatim code` `` | `verbatim code` |

## Headings and Links

-   A heading is one or more [`#`]{.b .blue} at the start of a line
    -   `# Header 1`, then `## Header 2`, then `### Header 3`
    -   More hashes means a [smaller, deeper]{.b .green} heading

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Links come in two forms:
    -   `<https://quarto.org>` shows the [bare URL]{.b .green}
    -   `[Quarto](https://quarto.org)` shows [text you pick]{.b .green}
:::

## Images and Lists

-   An image is a link with a [`!`]{.b .blue} in front of it
    -   `![Caption](elephant.png)`

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Lists are `*` or `-` for [unordered]{.b .blue}, numbers for [ordered]{.b .blue}
    -   Indent by four spaces to make a [sub-item]{.b .green}
:::
